reading.title: The Sliding Stones of Death Valley
reading.purpose: Read how scientists solved a mystery about rocks that move across a dry lake bed.
paras: In a dry lake bed in Death Valley National Park, California, visitors marvel at a strange sight. Rocks, some heavier than a grown person, sit at the ends of long trails that cross the flat, cracked mud. The rocks seem to have slid by themselves.

For many years, no one saw one move, and the sliding stones became an enigma, a mystery that scientists could not explain. The puzzle fascinated people around the world. Some thought strong winds did it, and others blamed ice. Every idea left questions, and the question baffled even careful observers.

Researchers began to ponder the problem. A few had a hunch, a feeling that winter ice might be the answer, even though they had no proof yet. To test the idea, a team placed GPS trackers inside some rocks and set up cameras.

In 2014, the team reported what they had seen. After a rare rain, a thin layer of water had covered the lake bed and frozen into floating sheets of ice. When the ice broke into panels, light winds pushed the panels, and the panels nudged the rocks along very slowly. With each careful measurement, the mystery began to unravel.

Today the puzzle is no longer a riddle, but the stones still fill visitors with awe. A solved mystery can intrigue us as much as an unsolved one, because it shows how much patient watching can reveal.

a rock that has been pushed by strong winds

qs.why: The text calls the sliding stones "a mystery that scientists could not explain."

qs.q: Which sentence tells how the ice helped move the rocks?
choices: In 2014, the team reported what they had seen.
After a rare rain, a thin layer of water had covered the lake bed and frozen into floating sheets of ice.
With each careful measurement, the mystery began to unravel.
When the ice broke into panels, light winds pushed the panels, and the panels nudged the rocks along very slowly.
qs.why: This sentence shows the chain: broken ice panels, pushed by wind, nudge the rocks along.

ev.text: When the ice broke into panels, light winds pushed the panels, and the panels nudged the rocks along very slowly.

qs.q: Why did the team put GPS trackers in some rocks and set up cameras?
choices: They wanted to move the rocks to a different place in the park.
They wanted to watch the rocks and record how they moved.
They hoped to prove that visitors had been moving the rocks.
They needed to find out how much each rock weighed.
qs.why: The team had a hunch about ice and needed to observe the rocks closely to test it.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Visitors to Death Valley should never walk near the rocks.
Strong winds alone are able to push any rock across mud.
Careful watching helped scientists solve a mystery.
Ice forms on every dry lake bed in the park each winter.
qs.why: The reading describes a mystery and how patient observation with trackers and cameras solved it.

needsReview.reason: Fact check: Racetrack Playa, Death Valley National Park; 'some heavier than a grown person' (documented stones exceed 100 pounds) and 'cracked mud' are standard descriptions.
Fact check: the 2014 PLOS ONE study (Norris et al.) with GPS-equipped rocks and time-lapse cameras reported thin ice panels pushed by light wind. Simplified for grade 5.
